analysis.investment_thesis: PDP Shipping fails the Magic Formula's "good business" test decisively — a 0.17% ROE indicates essentially no return on capital, making the apparent cheapness (P/E 5.97) meaningless. A cheap stock with near-zero returns on capital is a value trap, not a Magic Formula candidate.
key_strengths: Low headline P/E of 5.97 suggests optically cheap valuation
High promoter holding at 69.61% indicates skin in the game
Asset-light logistics model typically needs low capex
key_risks: ROE of 0.17% implies near-zero return on capital — fails Magic Formula quality screen
Micro-cap at INR 16.7 Cr — illiquid, easily manipulated, no institutional coverage
Commoditized freight-forwarding industry with no structural moat
red_flags: ROE 0.17% inconsistent with P/E 5.97 — suggests data quality issue or one-time earnings bump
Cannot compute EBIT/EV or ROIC reliably from disclosed metrics
Tiny market cap + recent BSE listing (2024) typical of speculative micro-caps
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks on two axes: earnings yield (cheap?) and return on capital (good?). PDP Shipping scores acceptably on the first dimension — P/E 5.97 would translate to an earnings yield around 16-17% if taken at face value — but it fails catastrophically on the second. A 0.17% ROE means the business earns essentially nothing on shareholder capital; ROIC on total capital employed is almost certainly in the low single digits at best. Greenblatt's entire thesis is that you want cheap AND good. Cheap alone is how you buy into capital-destroying businesses that stay cheap forever.

The numbers also don't reconcile cleanly: a P/E of ~6 with ROE of 0.17% implies P/B near 0.01, which is absurd, pointing to either trailing earnings distorted by a one-off item, or stale/inconsistent data. Combined with a INR 16.7 Cr market cap in a commoditized logistics sub-industry with no evident competitive advantage, this is exactly the type of name the systematic Magic Formula would screen out. Avoid.
